Title: Silymarin in non-alcoholic steatohepatitis – a new kid on the block ?

In this edition of Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology,  Chan et al. [1] report on the efficacy and 
safety of the herbal product Silymarin (SM)  in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 
single-center trial in patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).  
SM is the extract of the Silybum marianum (milk thistle) and contains a complex mixture of seven 
flavonolignans and a flavonoid [2]. Among all ingredients, silybinin is the most relevant one with the 
most important biological effects. The healing effects of this plant on the liver were first reported in 
the Ancient Egyptian Age [3]. When administered orally, SM has a low bioavailability due to  
inefficient absorption in the intestine and high first pass metabolism. However, by complexing SM 
with phosphatidylcholine the absorption and solubility has been improved, so that it can be 
effectively used as an intravenous (i.v) as well as oral formulation. Various in vitro and in vivo studies 
have shown that Silymarin has various beneficial effects on liver, such as anti-inflammatory, anti-
oxidant and anti-fibrotic effects (Table 1) [4].

Currently, the main indication for the use of SM is in the treatment of Amanita phalloides- fungus 
intoxication. Here, SM mainly inhibits the binding of amatoxin to the hepatocyte. Additionally, SM  
was also shown to decrease the production of reactive oxygen radicals (ROS) [5] and inhibit further 
free-radicals producing enzymes such as xanthine oxidase and NADPH oxidase. Therefore, it might be 
also used in other intoxications as mitochondrial stress and the production of ROS are key factors in 
the hepatocyte damage due to intoxication [6]. 
Chronic hepatitis C is a major health burden.  From 2001 - 2011pegylated interferon plus ribavirin 
(P/R) was the standard of care for hepatitis C[7], however approximately 50 % of all patients failed 
P/R treatment. Silibinin was able to interfere with the viral lifecycle [8, 9] and also block hepatitis C 
virus (HCV) entry and therefore reduce the viral load [10]. SM has been successfully tested in various 
trials in P/R non-responders [11]. However, with the high cure rates (>90%) achieved today with the 
new direct acting antiviral agents (DAAs) the use of SM in chronic hepatitis C is outdated [12].  
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is currently one of the most common liver diseases 
worldwide, which affects nearly 25% of the global adult population [13]. NAFLD encompasses the 
benign form of non-alcoholic fatty liver (NAFL) as well as the more severe, progressive form of non-
alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). Over all, about 33% of all patients with NAFLD will progress to 
fibrosis and about 30% of these patients will further develop liver cirrhosis, often accompanied by 
various complications.  Patients with NAFLD are at a high risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma 
[14] [15] even in the absence of cirrhosis.  The pathogenesis of NASH is a complex interaction 
between genetic and environmental risk factors, such as obesity and overnutrition, which then leads 
to insulin resistance and a disrupted lipid metabolism with accumulation of free fatty acids (FFA) in 
the liver. Although NAFLD is a rising health burden, therapeutic options are still rare, but urgently 
needed.  
In animal studies, silymarin improved the metabolic dysfunction, mainly by activation of the farnesyl 
X receptor (FXR) as well as the insulin resistance, hepatic inflammation and hepatic steatosis [16-18].

By inhibition of the transcription factor nuclear-factor κB (NF- κB), which is an important 
transcriptome factor for genes involved in pro-inflammatory processes, SM could also reduce pro-
inflammatory signals, such as  tumor-necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha), interleukin-1 (IL-1) or 
interleukin-6 (IL-6) [19] and therefore improve the pro-inflammatory environment in NASH.  Hepatic 
FFAs are mainly oxidized by mitochondrial beta-oxidation and in a smaller part by beta-oxidation in 
the endoplasmatic reticulum (ER) and peroxisomes. Excessive beta-oxidation leads to oxidative stress 
in the mitochondria by overproduction of ROS as well as to ER-stress and mitochondrial dysfunction 
[20], which further enhance activation of pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic pathways. In animal 
studies, SM exerts its anti-oxidant activity due to different pathways [6]. It scavenges free radicals, 
improves pro-survival cell signaling as well as the electron-transport chain in the mitochondrion and 
thereby reduces production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). In addition, it inhibits further free-
radicals producing enzymes such as xanthine oxidase and NADPH oxidase. In in vitro models of 
hepatic fibrogenesis, SM decreases the PDGF-induced cell proliferation and migration as well as it 
reduces the TGF-beta induced de novo synthesis of collagen type 1 [21, 22]. Besides the potential 
antifibrotic properties, in vitro data showed anticarcinogenic properties by modulating different 
molecular patterns [4].  
So far, SM has only been tested as combination therapy with Vitamin E in a few trials for NASH 
patients [23, 24]. The current study is the first randomized trial of the use of Silymarin in biopsy-
proven NASH.  In total, 99 patients were randomized to receive either 700mg of SM per os or placebo 
for 48 weeks. The majority of patients included in this trial had type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and 
central obesity, the two most relevant comorbidities in NASH.  NASH resolved in 30% of patients in 
both groups (disappearance of ballooning, and disappearance or persistence of mild lobular 
inflammation) . The rate of NASH resolution was relatively high compared to recent trials, but there 
were no significant differences between both groups concerning reduction in lobular inflammation, 
hepatocyte ballooning and the NASH and NAFLD activity score (NAS) and therefore, the primary 
outcome was not achieved. However, SM significantly improved fibrosis in patients with NASH, even

in patients with higher stages of fibrosis (F2-F3), compared to placebo. This is a remarkable finding as 
there were no differences in the corresponding NAS-scores between the groups neither at baseline 
nor at the end of the study. Therefore, the significant improvement of fibrosis only in the SM-group 
may underline the anti-fibrotic properties of SM, which are independent of the overall-improvement 
of NASH. However, the distinct mechanisms underlying the anti-fibrotic effect will need further 
validation. In previous studies, SM has shown beneficial effects on the metabolic syndrome and 
T2DM [25]. However, there was no significant improvement in T2DM in patients on SM compared 
with those on placebo in this study. This might be explained by the missing information on weight 
loss as well as changes in types and dosages of other medications during the study period. Patients 
with NASH have a high risk for cardiovascular events. This is also reflected in this cohort as the overall 
rates of hypertension and dyslipidaemia were about 62% and 76%, respectively in all patients. With 
regard to this high cardiovascular risk, studies of NASH should also consider the cardiovascular safety 
and improvement of cardiovascular risk factors. In the present study by Chan et al (1), SM 
significantly improved triglyceride levels compared to placebo. There were no differences with 
regard to adverse (AE) and serious adverse events (SAE). One cardiovascular event occurred in each 
of the two study groups during the trial (myocardial infarction and hospitalization for percutaneous 
coronary intervention), which mainly reflects the high cardiovascular risk in these patients. Overall, 
SM was safe and well tolerated in these patients.  
In conclusion, this is the first study that showed the anti-fibrotic benefits of Silymarin in NASH. This 
study underlines the safety and tolerability of Silymarin, which may therefore be a potential future 
therapy for patients with NASH presumably in combination with other agents. However, both larger 
multicenter trials and basic research are needed to confirm these promising results and to better 
understand the underlying mechanisms.
